Styles / 03 / Pilot

Bauhaus

The visual language associated with the Bauhaus school (1919–1933): primary colors, circles, squares, and triangles, heavy rules, sans-serif and lowercase type, and objects designed for industrial production.

Constructive / Bold / Geometric / Experimental

Visual grammar

  • Primary triad. Red, yellow, and blue with black, white, and gray. Colors are flat and saturated.
  • Elementary shapes. Circles, squares, and triangles, alone or combined into figures and letters.
  • Sans-serif, often lowercase. Geometric or grotesque letters. Herbert Bayer’s universal alphabet (1925) removed capitals.
  • Bars and rules. Thick black bars divide and direct the page. Diagonals add movement.
  • Asymmetric montage. Type, photographs, and shapes combine in dynamic, off-center compositions.
  • Honest materials. In objects: tubular steel, glass, metal, and plain wood, with visible construction.

What connects the references

Print carries most of the style’s graphic identity: Joost Schmidt’s 1923 exhibition poster and Offset cover, Moholy-Nagy’s Bauhausbücher, and Kandinsky’s exhibition postcard.

Objects show the same geometry in material: Marianne Brandt’s tea infuser, the Wagenfeld–Jucker lamp, and Breuer’s club chair. The Dessau building and Stölzl’s weaving design extend it to architecture and textile.

Measured evidence qualifies the “primary triad” in the grammar. Image measurements of the stored prints find one or two strong hues in most of them. The 1923 poster is red and black on paper, and only the Offset cover shows three. The triad is typical of later revivals, so the fingerprint, which asks for two or more hues, describes web implementations more than the historical print.

The Bauhaus100 site shows a 2019 web revival. The sites of the Bauhaus-Archiv and the Stiftung Bauhaus Dessau were captured too and not kept: photography and soft gradients carry them, not the Bauhaus grammar.

Lineage

  • Influenced by De Stijl. Theo van Doesburg taught informal De Stijl courses in Weimar in 1921–1922. The common reading is that primary color and orthogonal composition entered Bauhaus work through this contact.
  • Influenced by Constructivism. László Moholy-Nagy, who joined in 1923, brought constructivist photomontage and typography.
  • Related to International Typographic Style. The later Swiss style extends Bauhaus typography into a systematic grid method.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • Two or more primary colors appear as flat areas.
  • Circles, squares, or triangles are composition elements, not only icons.
  • Type is sans-serif, often bold or lowercase.
  • Heavy bars or rules organize the layout.

Rules it out

  • Pastel or muted palettes without primary accents.
  • Organic, ornamental, or script forms.
  • Gradients, gloss, or soft shadows.

Often confused with

Memphis
Memphis uses clashing, non-primary colors, patterns, and playful, irregular shapes. Bauhaus shapes are elementary and the palette is primary.
De Stijl
De Stijl allows only horizontal and vertical lines and rectangles. Bauhaus uses circles, triangles, and diagonals too.
International Typographic Style
The Swiss style is quieter: fewer colors, no decorative shapes, and a strict grid.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Use flat red, yellow, and blue on white or off-white, with black for text and bars.
  • Use large circles, squares, and triangles as layout elements, for example behind a heading.
  • Use a geometric sans-serif. Lowercase headings are appropriate.
  • Separate sections with thick black bars.
  • Break symmetry with one strong diagonal or off-center shape.

Keep the function

  • Do not use gradients, soft shadows, or rounded cards.
  • Do not add more than three hues beyond black, white, and gray.
  • Do not scatter shapes as random decoration. Each shape needs a place in the composition.

Useful directions: exhibitions, architecture and furniture studios, education, event posters.
